meta.title: Who really said "Only One Who Attempts the Absurd Is Capable of Achieving the Impossible"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein. Miguel de Unamuno wrote it in Spanish in 1905, in his commentary on Don Quixote — and we found the sentence in the scanned book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Only One Who Attempts the Absurd Is Capable of Achieving the Impossible'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is Miguel de Unamuno’s, from his 1905 Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho. Einstein was not attached to it until the 1990s.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually Miguel de Unamuno
answer.authorDates: 1864–1936 · Spanish philosopher, novelist, poet and rector of Salamanca
answer.sourceLine: Unamuno wrote it in Spanish in Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho (1905), his book-length commentary on Cervantes: “Sólo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible.” The English wording most people know comes from J. E. Crawford Flitch’s translation in Essays and Soliloquies (Knopf, 1925). Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive support for the attributions to Einstein or M. C. Escher.

source.excerpt: ¿Que es ello absurdo? — decís. ¿Y quién sabe qué es lo absurdo? ¡Y aunque lo fuera! Sólo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible. No hay más que un modo de dar una vez en el clavo, y es dar ciento en la herradura. Y sobre todo no hay más que un modo de triunfar de veras: arrostrar el ridículo.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ identifies the origin as Miguel de Unamuno’s Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho of 1905, quotes the Spanish, and concludes that “the linkages to Einstein and Escher are unsupported and appear to be spurious”.

We did not take that on trust. We downloaded the full scanned text of a Madrid: Renacimiento printing of 1914 ↗ from the Internet Archive and searched it: the sentence “Sólo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible” is there, in the passage about the man who carried sea-bream spawn to a Castilian pond — the same passage Flitch’s English renders. Note this is a later printing, not the first edition. Datings differ: Quote Investigator cites a 1905 first edition from Librería de Fernando Fe in Madrid, verified in Google Books Full View, while Wikipedia’s Unamuno bibliography dates the work 1914. We follow Quote Investigator, and flag the discrepancy rather than leave you to find it.

The English wording travelled through Essays and Soliloquies ↗, translated by J. E. Crawford Flitch and published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in 1925; the Internet Archive’s catalogue record confirms that edition. Burton Stevenson’s Home Book of Quotations reprinted it with a correct Unamuno credit in 1935.

Quote Investigator records that the poet Robin Morgan used the “she” variant in Sisterhood Is Global (1984) and expressly called it “a feminist proverb of indeterminate origin” — she claimed no authorship. The Einstein ascription appears by 1997, the Escher one by 2007.
source.excerptNote: Flitch’s 1925 English: “But it was absurd, you say? And who knows what is absurd and what is not? And even if it were! Only he who attempts the absurd is capable of achieving the impossible.” The passage is about a Salamanca man mocked for carrying sea-bream spawn inland to stock a pond in Castile — and making a fortune from it.

author.name: Miguel de Unamuno
author.heading: About Miguel de Unamuno
author.metaLine: 1864–1936 · Spanish philosopher, novelist, poet and playwright
author.bio: Miguel de Unamuno y Jugo was among the most forceful Spanish writers of his generation — a philosopher, novelist, poet and playwright who served twice as rector of the University of Salamanca. His central subject was the conflict between reason and the human refusal to accept oblivion, argued in Del sentimiento trágico de la vida (1913). Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho (1905) reads Cervantes’s novel as a spiritual text and treats Quixote’s willingness to look ridiculous as a virtue rather than a joke.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: One Spanish sentence about Don Quixote, later handed to three different people who did not write it.

items.why: Quote Investigator finds no substantive support ↗ for the linkage. Its earliest Einstein instance is from 1997, more than forty years after Einstein’s death and more than ninety years after Unamuno wrote the line.
The artist of impossible objects is an inviting home for a sentence about achieving the impossible, but the ascription is unsupported and only appears by 2007, in a book of lists.

Morgan’s group used the “Only she who attempts the absurd…” form in Sisterhood Is Global (1984), but she called it a feminist proverb of indeterminate origin ↗ rather than her own. She disclaimed credit; others assigned it to her anyway.
Written in Spanish in Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho (1905). We confirmed it in a scanned printing at the Internet Archive ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence belongs to Miguel de Unamuno, writing about Don Quixote in 1905 — as Quote Investigator concludes ↗ and as the scanned Spanish text confirms.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Unamuno was not writing a motivational slogan. He was arguing, through Cervantes, that his country’s real affliction was moral cowardice — the refusal to look ridiculous in defence of what you believe. The sentence lands as the payoff to a small, deliberately unglamorous story about a man mocked for stocking a Castilian pond with sea fish, who was right.

That is why the next line in the passage matters as much as the famous one: there is only one way of really triumphing, Unamuno writes, and it is to face ridicule. Detached from the Quixote commentary, the sentence becomes a graduation-speech flourish. In place, it is a rebuke.
detailsBody: The line reached a wide English-speaking audience through the theatre. Dale Wasserman, who wrote Man of La Mancha, said in his introduction to the published play that the motif of the attempt came from “another brilliant Miguel, Unamuno”, and quoted this sentence — correctly credited.

Quote Investigator traces the drift from there: an unattributed “she” variant at a 1974 women’s-club luncheon in Florida, a 1982 slogan T-shirt advertised in Mother Jones, the 1984 Sisterhood Is Global use, then Einstein in 1997 and Escher by 2007. At no point does anyone produce a source in Einstein’s writing.
context.pull: There is only one way of achieving a real triumph, and that is by facing ridicule with serenity.

sourcesVerified.claim: The adage originates with Miguel de Unamuno in 1905; the Einstein and Escher linkages are unsupported and appear spurious; Robin Morgan called it a feminist proverb of indeterminate origin.
The Spanish sentence "Solo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible" appears in the scanned full text of Vida de Don Quijote y Sancho (Madrid: Renacimiento, 1914).
Essays and Soliloquies by Miguel de Unamuno was published in New York by Knopf in 1925.
Miguel de Unamuno y Jugo lived 29 September 1864 to 31 December 1936 and was a Spanish essayist, novelist, poet, playwright and philosopher.
